title: Abdul El-Sayed Wins Michigan Democratic Senate Primary in Progressive Upset
excerpt: The progressive public health director defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in a razor-thin contest that tested the Democratic Party's ideological direction in a critical swing state.
body:
• Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Egyptian American former public health director, has won the Michigan Democratic Senate primary with 48.6% of the vote over moderate Rep. Haley Stevens
  • The race is widely seen as a bellwether for the Democratic Party's ideological direction, pitting progressive populism against establishment moderation in a critical swing state
  • El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers in November in a contest that could determine control of the U.S. Senate
  • Michigan's large Arab American community and shifting Democratic attitudes on Israel made the race a national flashpoint

Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old progressive and former Wayne County public health director, has won the Michigan Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, defeating four-term Rep. Haley Stevens in a razor-thin contest that tested the ideological fault lines running through the Democratic Party.

With 95% of the estimated vote tabulated early Wednesday, El-Sayed led Stevens 48.6% to 47.4%, according to the Associated Press. His campaign declared victory Wednesday morning. "Michiganders have spoken," said campaign manager Alia Kapasi in a statement.

A Defining Contest for Democratic Identity

The race had been billed as one of the clearest tests of the Democratic Party's direction since its 2024 presidential defeat. El-Sayed, backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and progressive groups, ran on a platform of universal healthcare, expanded abortion access, and sharp criticism of U.S. support for Israel. Stevens, supported by the Democratic establishment, the Congressional Black Caucus PAC, and pro-Israel groups including AIPAC-affiliated organizations, represented the party's moderate wing.

"Whatever happens tonight, we have a responsibility to assure that we unite."

— Abdul El-Sayed, in his election-night speech

A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found that self-described liberals now make up 71% of Democrats, up from 55% in 2012, while only 16% of Democrats backed continued military and economic aid to Israel. Those numbers help explain El-Sayed's edge in a state home to one of the country's largest Arab American communities.

The November Battle Ahead

El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers, a former U.S. Representative who ran uncontested in his primary, in November's general election. Rogers narrowly lost a previous Senate bid to Democrat Elissa Slotkin in 2024 and has expressed confidence about facing El-Sayed, telling CNN, "I think he's so radical. I think he's going to lose big parts of the west part of the state."

The Michigan seat is critical to Democratic hopes of regaining Senate control. Incumbent Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is not seeking a third term, making this the only open Democratic-held Senate seat in a state won by Donald Trump in 2024. Republicans have not won a Senate race in Michigan since 1994.

A Diaspora Milestone

El-Sayed's victory marks a significant moment for immigrant communities in American politics. The son of Egyptian immigrants, his progressive coalition drew heavily from young voters—those under 50 broke for him by 42 percentage points, according to Emerson College polling—and from Michigan's diverse immigrant communities who see his candidacy as a repudiation of establishment politics.

An Emerson survey had shown El-Sayed leading 54% to 39% among likely Democratic primary voters, with independents breaking for him by a 27-point margin. The actual margin proved significantly tighter, with Stevens showing strength in Detroit and Wayne County.

What's Next

Both candidates struck unity tones in their early-morning speeches. Stevens told supporters she was "feeling good" about the race, while El-Sayed called on Democrats to "send a blow to Trumpism" by defeating Rogers in November. The race is likely to be scrutinized by prospective 2028 presidential contenders searching for a message to reconnect with voters, according to Reuters.
